rv.q: It's an energetic, necessary tour de force for the actor.
A gloriously loud love letter to a place where clubbers once flocked from mining villages to escape and be who they wanted to be.
There's humour sure, but the anger at the hand dealt to Lindsay, Terry and Jen is the stronger theme.

Phillips has used the testimonies of 30 locals from Doncaster to paint a vivid portrait of her city in the 1990s. Working-class life where moving on is not accessible or sought after, living for the moment the norm, for the weekend high of excess alcohol and dancing (‘being in Karisma is like wearing a disguise’).

But this isn’t only a “remember the 90s” party piece. That first club entry becomes the gateway to a much messier story of escapism. One triumphant night spirals into a year‑long bender, tipping from self‑discovery into self‑destruction until a particularly chaotic evening forces Lindsay to face the music.

cn.t: Critics praise this energetic love letter to club culture and self-discovery, though some find the anger overshadows the humor. A necessary tour de force that captures both escape and frustration.
